segments.title: How selective cheating kept the Washington Treaty alive
segments.body: The counterfactual starts from the view that every signatory exploited some favourable treaty language, while no navy used every available device. Selective restraint helped preserve the Washington system despite departures from the intended spirit of its rules. The premise removes that restraint and extends evasion across the available treaty openings. In this scenario, a later London agreement would either fail or contain so many exceptions that it could impose little effective restraint.

evidence.note: The all-powers-cheat premise, selective historical evasion, and the prediction of an ineffective or abandoned London settlement.

segments.summary: The counterfactual starts with selective treaty evasion and asks what changes when every naval power uses every available loophole.

segments.title: Tiger, Hood, and the battlecruiser spectrum
segments.body: In this classification, HMS Tiger is a more substantial battlecruiser than the original Renown and Repulse designs, which began as Fisher's lighter ships and were later modernized. Tiger also has the greater standard displacement. Scaling Tiger to Hood's size would produce a much heavier ship. Hood's armour and subdivision fall well short of the fast-battleship standard used in this comparison, while Tiger offers the better example of a battlecruiser moving in that direction. The Queen Elizabeth class approaches the same design problem from the battleship side.

evidence.note: Tiger's greater standard displacement than Renown and Repulse, the scaled comparison with Hood, and contrasting routes toward a fast battleship.

segments.summary: HMS Tiger, Renown and Repulse, Hood, and the Queen Elizabeth class show why protection and design ancestry matter when classifying battlecruisers.

segments.title: How standard displacement could hide wartime weight
segments.body: Standard displacement includes the ship's declared wartime outfit, ammunition, provisions, and crew water, but excludes fuel and reserve feed water. Reserve feed water can therefore contribute protection without entering the measured total. Another proposed evasion rests on the word intended: a navy could declare half-filled magazines while building space for a larger load. Actual wartime ammunition expenditure is used to challenge the idea that declared allowances described every ship's operational load. Extra wartime weapons and crews widen that difference further.

evidence.note: Standard displacement includes the declared wartime outfit but excludes fuel and reserve feed water, leaving ammunition and manning open to manipulation.

segments.summary: Excluding fuel and reserve feed water creates one opening, while declared wartime ammunition and manning create others.

segments.title: Light peacetime armour on a hull prepared for war
segments.body: County-class cruisers provide the example of ships prepared to receive 4-inch armour plates held ashore. The proposed extension is a battleship with an 8-inch peacetime belt and heavier 13-, 14-, or 15-inch plates ready for war. Its hull would need the displacement capacity and internal subdivision for that heavier condition from the outset. The risk is accepting reduced protection while relying on sufficient warning to fit the armour. Outright understatement is another possibility because a 35,000-ton ship and a 36,000-ton ship would be difficult to distinguish by appearance. Declared intentions could also change with a successor in command.

evidence.note: County armour stocks, proposed replaceable belts, structural preparation, mobilization risk, and the difficulty of judging small displacement differences by sight.

segments.summary: A lightly armoured peacetime ship could retain the subdivision and weight capacity needed for a much heavier wartime belt.

segments.title: Carrier definitions leave aviation weight open to argument
segments.body: The treaty defines a carrier through displacement, aviation purpose, the ability to launch and recover aircraft, and permitted armament. A carrier could nevertheless be prepared for armour and defensive guns that it did not carry in peace. Onboard cranes and machinery would help install those fittings, while an escort could provide protection during the transition to war. Changing aircraft weights also open an argument for excluding aircraft from standard displacement. Extending that argument to aviation stores, personnel, and their supplies would free still more declared tonnage. These are proposed readings of the treaty's wording that depart from its intended spirit.

evidence.note: Carrier definitions, cranes and escorts during mobilization, and proposed exclusions for aircraft and their supporting outfit.

segments.summary: The carrier rules invite disputes over peacetime weapons, removable armour, aircraft stores, and the personnel supporting the air group.

segments.title: Why mutual cheating discouraged formal accusations
segments.body: Without a treaty court, enforcement depends on what the signatories are willing to challenge. The account of an overweight Italian cruiser in a British dry dock pairs British silence with foreign awareness of Royal Navy armour stocks. Japanese acceptance of the Lexington conversions is likewise linked to questionable features of Akagi and Kaga. A formal accusation would expose the accuser's own practices. Extending that reciprocal vulnerability to every loophole is the proposed reason all-out evasion could continue without formal complaints.

evidence.note: The absence of a treaty court and examples of reciprocal tolerance involving Italian cruisers, British armour stocks, and American and Japanese carriers.

segments.summary: Without a treaty court, reciprocal knowledge of undeclared weight made public enforcement politically dangerous for every signatory.

segments.title: Auxiliaries designed for rapid carrier conversion
segments.body: A nominal minelaying auxiliary could be designed around a future flight deck and hangar. Its superstructure and funnels would be arranged for movement to the side. Mines, boats, or guns could initially obstruct the deck, while the space intended for a hangar served as a mine store. At mobilization, removing those obstructions would reveal a carrier layout prepared in advance. The conversion could then be presented as an unexpected dockyard achievement.

evidence.note: A hypothetical minelaying auxiliary with movable superstructure and funnels, a future hangar used for mines, and an initially obstructed deck.

segments.summary: A nominal minelayer or auxiliary could be laid out so that a dockyard could turn it into an aircraft carrier soon after mobilization.

segments.title: How early carriers recovered aircraft with little machinery
segments.body: Early carriers needed fewer specialized fittings than later ships. The examples here have no catapults, and their arresting wires, where fitted, run lengthwise along the deck. Those wires are intended to keep a landing aircraft from being blown over the side. Flight-deck crews still catch aircraft by their wings, with naval aircraft strengthened for that handling. This comparatively simple recovery arrangement supports the proposed rapid conversion of auxiliaries into carriers.

evidence.note: Early catapult absence, longitudinal wires for lateral restraint, and flight-deck crews catching reinforced aircraft wings.

segments.summary: Longitudinal wires and crews grabbing strengthened wings illustrate how limited early carrier recovery equipment could be.

segments.title: The sub-10,000-ton carrier escape hatch
segments.body: HMS Hermes displaced only a little more than 10,000 tons under an honest calculation. Omitting defensive weapons, their crews, ammunition, and supporting stores could bring a similar design beneath the treaty definition. Ships below that threshold did not consume the national carrier-tonnage allowance. A navy could therefore attach small scouting carriers to cruiser groups while reserving its counted tonnage for large fleet strike carriers. The loophole changes carrier force structure rather than merely changing one ship's specification. Moving scouting aircraft to those carriers would also free deck space and weight on the cruisers, whose seaplanes were a less effective aviation arrangement.

evidence.note: Hermes-based displacement reductions, small carriers outside the cumulative allowance, and transferring aviation weight from cruisers to scouting carriers.

segments.summary: A creatively measured Hermes-sized carrier could fall below the threshold and escape the cumulative carrier-tonnage allowance.

segments.title: What each navy historically chose to bend
segments.body: The scenario depends on governments paying for wider evasion. Its historical examples include British County-class cruisers, American Lexington conversions and submarines, Italian heavy cruisers, and French destroyers and cruisers. In the Japanese case, aggressive efforts to save weight and exploit materials are linked to ships getting into trouble in storms. Japan's subsequent move toward outright cheating follows that warning about pushing lightweight construction too far. The alternate history extends those selected practices across more of each navy's construction.

evidence.note: The funding assumption, selected national examples, and Japanese storm trouble associated with excessive weight saving.

segments.summary: The historical baseline was selective evasion: Britain, the United States, Italy, France, and Japan each concentrated on different ship types or measurements.

segments.title: Cruiser turrets shared with coastal batteries
segments.body: A common barbette could accept either an 8-inch turret or a twin 9.2-inch mounting. Building the larger turrets for coastal batteries would put replacement weapons in service ashore before war. Common turret manufacture could also be defended as an economy that kept yards and industry working. Lifting out a whole turret and fitting another is judged less demanding than changing guns and breeches within the mounting. Magazines would need enough spare space for the larger shells. The proposal depends on designing that compatibility into the ship.

evidence.note: Proposed common barbette and magazine arrangements for 8-inch and 9.2-inch turrets, with coastal batteries providing reserve mountings.

segments.summary: A cruiser could carry 8-inch guns in peace while using barbettes and magazines prepared for replacement 9.2-inch turrets.

segments.title: Keeping condemned warships available through other uses
segments.body: Apart from the Article 9 carrier-conversion exception, the scrapping provision forbids reconverting a designated ship into a warship. The proposed evasions exploit the time and other uses between designation and final destruction. A hull could become a coastguard asset or a training establishment attached to land. A scrapyard could also leave it afloat for years. First World War ships that lingered into the mid-1930s illustrate how delayed disposal might leave a hull available close to another war, although their later reactivation is a hypothetical possibility.

evidence.note: The reconversion prohibition, alternative uses, and ships waiting many years for scrapping.

segments.summary: Training use and slow scrapping could preserve old hulls even after a treaty designated them for disposal.

segments.title: Preparing cruiser guns and protection for mobilization
segments.body: A triple 6-inch turret might leave enough room for a twin 8-inch or 9.2-inch replacement. Transferring aviation to a supporting cruiser carrier would free deck space and weight for other purposes. Stored armour and feed water used for torpedo protection offer further ways to prepare a heavier wartime ship. Single 4-inch peacetime guns could give way to twin anti-aircraft mountings kept ashore as harbour defences. Rapid fitting would depend on compatible arrangements, large cranes, and crews able to make the change. The short conversion time imagined here follows from that advance preparation.

evidence.note: Triple 6-inch and twin heavier-gun alternatives, transferred aviation, reserve armour, feed-water protection, and single-to-twin 4-inch gun changes.

segments.summary: Common turret spaces, shore-held anti-aircraft guns, and transferred scouting aircraft could support a heavier wartime cruiser.

segments.title: Using gun liners to preserve a larger wartime calibre
segments.body: The capital-ship gun proposal starts with a 16.5-inch barrel fitted with an extra-thick liner that reduces its bore to 16 inches. A normal liner could restore the larger calibre in war. Alternatively, coastal batteries using matching larger guns could provide replacement barrels and ammunition already held ashore. Common manufacture would supply an economical explanation for the barrel's dimensions. The argument turns on the calibre actually carried in peace, while the larger wartime outfit remains a prepared option.

evidence.note: The proposed thick liner reducing a 16.5-inch barrel to 16 inches, with larger shore guns and ammunition supporting later conversion.

segments.summary: A thick liner could make a 16.5-inch barrel fire a treaty-compliant 16-inch shell while preserving a later conversion option.

segments.title: Why electric drive helps a ship accept extra machinery
segments.body: A compartment declared as storage could be sized for additional boilers or a turbine. Boilers are the easier addition when another turbine would require alignment with a propeller shaft. Turbo-electric drive changes that constraint because electric motors turn the shafts. Extra generating machinery can then feed the propulsion system without adding another direct mechanical connection to a shaft. The resulting speed increase remains conditional on available hull space and a ship designed to use the extra power.

evidence.note: Storage spaces reserved for machinery, shaft-alignment difficulties, and the proposed flexibility of turbo-electric drive.

segments.summary: Reserved machinery space is easier to exploit when turbo-electric propulsion separates turbines from the propeller shafts.

segments.title: The ten-year peace assumption nobody trusted
segments.body: Reserve fittings and machinery require confidence that mobilization time will be available. In this interpretation, navies avoided some of those preparations because they did not truly believe the ten-year peace assumption behind contemporary planning. Governments therefore restricted fleets in the name of lasting peace while behaving as if another crisis could arrive sooner. That contradiction amounted to a failure of national-security leadership rather than a narrow technical choice.

evidence.note: The interpretation that disbelief in ten years of peace discouraged mobilization preparations, despite publicly accepted treaty restraint.

segments.summary: The navies accepted treaty restraint and a ten-year planning rule while declining preparations that only made sense if they believed peace would last.

segments.title: G3 conversions anchor a five-carrier strike force
segments.body: The conversion clause allows two carriers of up to 33,000 tons from ships otherwise due for scrapping. In the proposed British case, G3 hulls treated as barely started conversions would leave few inherited design compromises. Hangars could follow Eagle and Hermes, while machinery ducting and uptakes could be arranged from the outset. Two declared 33,000-ton ships would use 66,000 tons of the 135,000-ton carrier allowance. The remaining allowance would support three carriers of about 23,000 tons. Small carriers outside the counted allowance would supply the extra flight decks needed for cruising duties and overseas presence.

evidence.note: The two-carrier conversion clause, minimally started G3 hulls, new hangar and uptake arrangements, and a five-carrier allocation supported by small scouting carriers.

segments.summary: Two declared 33,000-ton G3 conversions and three roughly 23,000-ton ships could form a five-carrier striking force.

segments.title: A separate proposal for five declared 27,000-ton carriers
segments.body: A more aggressive alternative would declare the G3-derived carriers at 27,000 tons even though the conversion clause permitted larger ships. Three more carriers at the same declared displacement would bring the total to 135,000 tons. The design argument treats 27,000 tons as enough for the large air group sought by American designers and the armour sought by British designers. Building all counted carriers at that size still limits the number of available flight decks. The scheme therefore continues to rely on smaller carriers outside the cumulative allowance for routine overseas work.

evidence.note: An alternative five-by-27,000-ton declaration and the claimed combination of air-group capacity and armour at that size.

segments.summary: Declaring every large carrier at 27,000 tons would fit five ships within 135,000 tons, with small carriers providing additional flight decks.

segments.title: Why words like designed and intended create diplomatic latitude
segments.body: Diplomatic wording can leave signatories room to tolerate conduct they would otherwise need to confront. Terms such as designed and intended state a purpose without proving the limits of a vessel's physical capabilities. The London Treaty example imagines an auxiliary with minelaying fittings that could later accept torpedo tubes. Boiler limiters could hold its peacetime speed down until war. The British sloop example concerns limiters removed in wartime. Such latitude gives governments an argument for overlooking a disputed practice while maintaining an agreement. The interpretation links engineering opportunities to a political wish to avoid confrontation.

evidence.note: Diplomatic latitude, purpose-based wording, and proposed auxiliary minelaying or torpedo fittings and speed limiters.

segments.summary: Diplomatic language can preserve peace by leaving governments room to overlook dual-use machinery, weapons, and performance.

segments.title: Cruiser carriers scout for dispersed naval stations
segments.body: Ryujo's attempt to compress a fleet carrier into an extremely light hull provides the unsuitable model. A cruiser-carrier alternative would carry roughly 24 to 30 aircraft for scouting, local air defence, torpedo attack, and light bombing. One such ship could accompany four to six cruisers or serve a Royal Navy station without consuming space and weight aboard every cruiser. Regular construction alongside County-class groups would spread aviation across the fleet. Once Britain demonstrated the type, the United States, Japan, and possibly France would have strong reasons to follow.

evidence.note: A cruiser carrier with 24-30 aircraft, roughly one per four to six cruisers, station service, and likely foreign imitation.

segments.summary: A practical small carrier would support four to six cruisers with fighters and multipurpose scouts rather than imitate an overloaded fleet carrier.

segments.title: Escort-carrier thinking before the Second World War
segments.body: HMS Argus and First World War merchant conversions provide precedents for the later escort-carrier concept. British writing in the 1920s and 1930s envisaged merchant hulls supporting cruiser and escort operations. In this account, later claims to have invented the type obscure that earlier work. The accompanying criticism separates credit for the idea from the Royal Navy's practical desire to obtain converted ships.

evidence.note: HMS Argus, First World War merchant conversions, and interwar British writing on cruiser and escort carriers.

segments.summary: HMS Argus, First World War merchant conversions, and later Royal Navy studies place the escort-carrier idea well before its wartime mass use.

segments.title: Small-carrier fleets complicate later tonnage limits
segments.body: A navy with several useful small carriers would resist a later agreement that counted them against its main allowance. Five ships declared at 8,000 tons each would absorb 40,000 tons. If declared nearer 9,500 tons apiece, they would take still more of the allowance. The proposed obstacle to a new treaty therefore grows as the ships enter service: a previously exempt capability becomes something its owners want to keep.

evidence.note: Five existing small carriers, their combined declared tonnage, and the predicted refusal to include them in a later carrier allowance.

segments.summary: Once small carriers enter service, counting their combined tonnage in a successor treaty becomes harder for their owners to accept.

segments.title: British debt repayment and the end of rolling infrastructure investment
segments.body: In this economic interpretation, Britain could still afford shipbuilding after the First World War while prioritizing repayment of its war debt. The deeper financial difficulties accumulate through the First World War, the Great Depression, the Second World War, and the abrupt end of Lend-Lease, alongside poor financial governance. A separate criticism concerns the suspension of continuing infrastructure investment in the 1920s and 1930s. Dry-dock expansion and other improvements inherited from the Victorian pattern gave way to projects approved when a particular need arose. That change from regular investment to individual decisions stored up problems for later decades.

evidence.note: The interpretation of postwar debt repayment, cumulative economic shocks, and the shift from rolling infrastructure investment to individual projects.

segments.summary: The economic argument distinguishes Britain's immediate postwar debt burden from the cumulative shocks and investment cuts that followed.

segments.title: Serial small carriers accelerate doctrine and design
segments.body: Small carriers would be built more frequently than fleet carriers, providing more opportunities to test operating ideas. The fewer large ships would remain prestige assets while cruiser carriers became ordinary experimental platforms. In this scenario, Britain might avoid separating its large carriers into heavily armoured ships operating close to the fleet and strike carriers operating farther away. The close-fleet role includes the Mediterranean and South China Sea, while the distant strike role emphasizes large attacks on fleets in harbour. American carriers could likewise gain armour and torpedo protection while retaining large air groups if the schemes released enough usable tonnage.

evidence.note: Frequent small-carrier construction as an experimental programme, British close-fleet and distant-strike roles, and American protection and air-group tradeoffs.

segments.summary: Repeated cruiser-carrier construction would provide experimental flight decks and reduce the need to choose between carrier armour and air-group size.

segments.title: New-ship declarations and protective feed-water tanks
segments.body: New ships offer more room to manipulate declared ammunition than familiar Queen Elizabeth- or R-class battleships. An allowance of only 100 rounds per gun is imagined for ships designed to take more. Reserve feed-water tanks could occupy otherwise unarmoured spaces, where the water absorbs and spreads some impact energy and the tank adds subdivision. Armour fitted in war could then sit outside that liquid layer. The water could also be drained to reduce draft and increase speed. These are proposed uses of excluded weight, with the protective benefit and operating condition changing together.

evidence.note: New-build ammunition understatement compared with familiar existing ships, and reserve feed-water tanks as protection, subdivision, and adjustable weight.

segments.summary: New hulls offer more freedom to understate ammunition, while reserve feed-water tanks could add protection and adjustable weight.

segments.title: Dockyard investment makes rapid refitting possible
segments.body: Rapid armour installation and gun changes require cranes, warehouses, and stores in the right places. Navies with worldwide facilities would begin with an advantage. Others would need to build the supporting infrastructure before the conversion schemes became practical. Merchant handling facilities and dry docks could also serve warships. Subsidies or reduced taxes could encourage civilian construction of facilities useful to naval mobilization.

evidence.note: Geographical differences in dockyard capacity and proposed merchant facilities supported through subsidies or tax incentives.

segments.summary: Stored weapons and armour become useful only when suitable cranes, stores, and docks can support refits where they are needed.

segments.title: Greater naval confidence could open diplomatic discussions
segments.body: In the counterfactual, widespread evasion could make each navy feel less constrained by the treaty. Japan might feel less singled out if it obtained the capability it wanted while other powers did the same. Existing talks would then provide time to address problems beyond naval limits. The expectation still rules out a durable renewal of the same treaty system. Better relations and more concerted efforts remain possible, although the argument expressly doubts that discussion would solve every problem given the paths individual powers were taking.

evidence.note: The hypothesis that reciprocal evasion reduces resentment and opens time for broader diplomacy, with explicit doubt that it can solve every problem.

segments.summary: If every signatory feels less constrained, the treaty conference may create a period for wider negotiation even without producing a durable successor agreement.

segments.title: American participation and the argument for naval presence
segments.body: The naval conferences bring other powers into group discussions with the United States, which chose not to join the League of Nations despite Wilson's support for its creation. Dr. Clarke treats that absence and limited military investment as reasons American diplomatic influence fell short of its potential after the First World War. His wider argument is that representatives, ships, and people at the scene give a state a practical role in events. Declarations issued from a distance cannot substitute for that participation in this interpretation. The same principle is applied to small and large powers.

evidence.note: American non-membership of the League and Dr. Clarke's interpretation connecting presence and military investment with diplomatic influence.

segments.summary: The American decision to stay outside the League introduces an argument about the influence gained by sustained diplomatic and naval participation.

segments.title: An F3-style fast capital ship prepared for extra armour
segments.body: Britain could pursue an F3-style ship as a battlecruiser or lightly armoured battleship. The proposed speed is 28 knots with 16-inch guns. A longer hull would retain substantial internal subdivision while allowing armour to be added later. The F3 arrangement also changes the relative height of the forward gun positions and the disposition of supporting weapons. Its attraction is the combination of speed and prepared protection within the scenario's manipulated peacetime condition.

evidence.note: The proposed F3-style 28-knot capital ship with 16-inch guns, a longer hull, internal subdivision, and armour that could be added later.

segments.summary: The British proposal combines 28 knots and 16-inch guns with a longer hull and protection designed to grow in war.

segments.title: F3 appearance as a personal argument about naval presence
segments.body: The F3 layout is preferred here for its appearance as a ship representing Britain overseas. The comparison is with the all-forward Nelson and Rodney arrangement, whose efficiency is appreciated despite its unusual proportions. Two large oblong funnels would have supplied a familiar British visual signature, although neither the F3 design nor Nelson and Rodney had that arrangement. The preference for the F3's shape is explicitly aesthetic. It supports an argument that an imposing appearance matters in diplomacy even when the compared ships are both capable.

evidence.note: Aesthetic comparison with Nelson and Rodney, the wished-for British two-funnel signature, and the claim that appearance affects naval presence.

segments.summary: The preference for F3's proportions concerns how a capital ship looks during overseas presence missions.

segments.title: Could replacing Tiger justify a third British capital ship?
segments.body: Giving up Tiger offers another proposed route to a larger British building programme. The suggestion is to invoke First World War damage and argue for a third replacement. Calling the new vessels battlecruisers would supply a further justification for the claim. They would actually be lightly armoured capital ships prepared for rapid increases in protection. The possibility remains conditional on persuading the other powers to accept that interpretation.

evidence.note: A hypothetical Tiger replacement claim, its First World War damage pretext, and lightly armoured ships prepared for heavier protection.

segments.summary: The proposed sacrifice of Tiger uses claimed war damage and replacement needs to seek a third new capital ship.

segments.title: Why Lexington's 8-inch guns waste carrier capacity
segments.body: Lexington's 8-inch batteries sit high and to one side, creating topweight and balancing penalties as well as demands for magazines and ammunition handling. The design preference here is to put those guns on a separate escorting cruiser. Washington's rules leave cruiser numbers uncapped, so the proposed alternative depends on obtaining the construction budget. Removing the heavy carrier batteries would free tonnage for the ship's other requirements. Dr. Clarke attributes the historical compromise to congressional and Treasury budget pressure, while strongly preferring additional cruisers to the carrier-mounted guns.

evidence.note: Lexington's high, off-centre 8-inch batteries and their balance and ammunition-handling costs, alongside the preference for cruiser escorts and the budget explanation.

segments.summary: Removing Lexington's heavy side-mounted batteries would reduce topweight, ballast, magazines, and crew demands when cruiser construction was still unlimited.

segments.title: A faster replacement for the lost Amagi conversion
segments.body: The loss of Amagi's battlecruiser hull in an earthquake leaves Japan converting the battleship Kaga. The preferred counterfactual alternative is to claim another battlecruiser hull for conversion or rebuild the battleship hull from near the keel into a faster form. The means of securing that replacement hull remain unresolved. Trials aboard Furious are offered as contemporary evidence that Japan already knew speed helped aircraft launch and operate with heavier loads. That evidence supplies the argument against accepting a slower hull without requiring knowledge of later carrier warfare.

evidence.note: Amagi's loss, Kaga's battleship origin, the proposed new or heavily rebuilt faster hull, and Japan's access to Furious trial lessons.

segments.summary: The proposed Japanese response is a faster hull, justified by contemporary trials linking ship speed to aircraft launch performance.

segments.title: Why Kaga's battleship hull weakens Japanese carrier doctrine
segments.body: The comparison gives Akagi a speed of 31.5 knots and Kaga 28 knots after the latter's 1935 modernization. Those extra 3.5 knots affect battle manoeuvres and wind over the flight deck. The quoted endurance figures also distinguish 10,000 nautical miles at 16 knots from the same distance at 15 knots. That one-knot difference is estimated to save roughly a day and a half to two days on a long passage. Japanese attrition doctrine makes distant operations important because they are intended to weaken the enemy before the decisive battle. Carrier mobility therefore matters both in launching aircraft and in reaching the earlier operations on which the final battle depends.

evidence.note: Akagi and Kaga speed and range figures, including Kaga's post-1935 condition, and mobility in attrition operations before decisive battle.

segments.summary: Akagi and Kaga illustrate how a few knots affect aircraft operations, long passages, and attrition before Japan's planned decisive battle.

segments.title: Using a capital-ship accident to unlock replacement tonnage
segments.body: The scenario treats accidental loss as a route to replacing an old capital ship. Its cynical extension is a deliberately arranged incident that damages an obsolete hull beyond repair. The imagined explanations include a collision with a merchant ship followed by impact against a rock. A captain already near retirement could bear the nominal disgrace, while insurance is jokingly invoked to meet part of the replacement cost. These are hypothetical procurement pretexts, without an identified historical accident offered as proof.

evidence.note: Hypothetical damage to an old capital ship, nominal blame for a retiring captain, and an imagined insurance contribution toward replacement.

segments.summary: An arranged accident is proposed as a cynical pretext for replacing an obsolete capital ship.

segments.title: Why Britain declined a Hermes-derived small carrier
segments.body: Dr. Clarke has found notes discussing a sub-10,000-ton carrier based on Hermes soon after Washington, but has not located a corresponding design. The proposal's advocates thought funding could be obtained. It could expand aircraft production for the Fleet Air Arm, then within the Royal Air Force, at a time when that relationship still seemed promising. The objection was the expectation that other navies would follow Britain's example. The notes therefore support consideration of the concept while leaving its detailed design uncertain.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke's account of notes on a small Hermes derivative, the absence of a located design, possible aviation funding, and concern that rivals would copy it.

segments.summary: A Hermes-derived small carrier was considered, but fear that rivals would copy it weighed against the concept.

segments.title: War-debt repayment and British reluctance to start a naval race
segments.body: The fiscal interpretation here makes debt repayment the British government's main postwar spending priority. It compares the cuts after the First World War with retrenchment after the Napoleonic Wars. Promises of social and welfare reform are contrasted with the money directed toward reducing debt. Avoiding a new naval race therefore fits a wider effort to limit government expenditure. Debt repayment therefore reinforces the objection to the small-carrier programme.

evidence.note: Political reluctance to fund a naval race and the comparison between debt-driven retrenchment after the First World War and the Napoleonic Wars.

segments.summary: The objection to another naval race forms part of an interpretation of British postwar spending as dominated by debt repayment.

segments.title: More competition in cruisers and small carriers
segments.body: The scenario expands competition below the 10,000-ton threshold in both cruisers and cruiser carriers. The British estimate is a small carrier every other year during the period. That would produce four or five Hermes-like vessels in addition to Hermes. An American programme is expected to be of a similar scale. The proposed increase is a sustained sequence of orders, with the number of small flight decks growing alongside cruiser construction.

evidence.note: A larger competition in cruisers and sub-10,000-ton carriers, with an estimate of four or five extra British Hermes-like ships and a comparable American programme.

segments.summary: The estimated British programme adds four or five Hermes-like ships, with the United States following at a comparable scale.

segments.title: Ryujo and the limits of a miniature fleet carrier
segments.body: Ryujo supplies the example of trying to put a fleet-carrier air group into a small hull. The attempted outfit is 48 aircraft, while making the ship viable brings its stated displacement up to 10,600 tons. The scenario expects Japan to try that demanding approach before recognizing the value of a more modest scout carrier. Aircraft and scouting duties already consume space and weight on Japanese cruisers and compromise their other work. Moving those duties to dedicated small carriers would address that problem. The United States is imagined reaching the same choice after its own unsuccessful attempt at a miniature fleet carrier.

evidence.note: The 48-aircraft ambition, growth to 10,600 tons, Japanese cruiser scouting burdens, and the imagined American and Japanese shift to scout carriers.

segments.summary: The Ryujo example links excessive air-group ambition to weight growth, then proposes small scout carriers to relieve cruiser aviation duties.

segments.title: Small flight decks as alternatives to seaplane carriers
segments.body: Wider construction by the leading naval powers could make small flight-deck carriers attractive elsewhere. Sweden is imagined building one in place of its seaplane-carrying cruiser. France could choose one or two instead of a seaplane carrier, and the Netherlands is another possible adopter. Italy might follow because other navies already possessed the type. These are proposed national responses to a visible example, with no single construction programme assumed for every country.

evidence.note: Possible small-carrier adoption by France, Sweden, and the Netherlands, with Italy following the example of other navies.

segments.summary: France, Sweden, and possibly the Netherlands could adopt small flight decks, while Italy might imitate them for prestige.

segments.title: Three new British fast ships change fleet comparisons
segments.body: Sacrificing Tiger might allow Britain to field three of the proposed fast capital ships. Each is imagined at 28 knots with nine 16-inch guns. An 8-inch peacetime belt would be prepared for replacement by 13- or 14-inch armour. Adding those ships to Hood would change the comparison facing American planners, who are described as already treating Hood as equivalent to a Colorado. The argument uses that altered balance to explain why other navies would want further construction.

evidence.note: The proposed British ship numbers, speed, nine-gun armament, armour changes, and comparison of Hood with Colorado.

segments.summary: Three hypothetical 28-knot ships with nine 16-inch guns and replaceable armour would alter American comparisons with the British fleet.

segments.title: A failed London settlement and continued shipbuilding
segments.body: In this scenario, the powers want more ships and no restrictive London naval agreement follows. They enter the next period with more carriers, probably more cruisers and destroyers, and cruisers prepared for quick gun changes. Higher construction rates during the 1920s preserve more infrastructure for further building. Early-1930s governments could then place ship orders as a means of providing employment during economic difficulty. The resulting fleets are expected to give those governments greater confidence in later crisis management.

evidence.note: The predicted failure of a London agreement, larger initial fleets, retained construction infrastructure, and shipbuilding as employment during the early-1930s economic crisis.

segments.summary: Continued 1920s construction could preserve infrastructure and leave more ships available before depression-era governments expand naval orders.

segments.title: Perceived weakness and the credibility of diplomatic warnings
segments.body: In this interpretation, Neville Chamberlain's appeasement partly reflects a belief that treaty-era disarmament left Britain unable to support its diplomatic words with sufficient force. The associated phrase is attributed to someone close to Chamberlain, and its exact wording is recalled uncertainly from memory. The argument concerns leaders' perception of weakness as well as the forces actually available. Warnings are expected to sound less convincing when their authors doubt their ability to act. The counterfactual therefore proposes that wider treaty evasion could have improved deterrence and helped preserve the peace the treaties sought.

evidence.note: Perceived British weakness and deterrence, with a phrase attributed to someone close to Chamberlain and an explicit warning that its wording is recalled from memory.

segments.summary: The argument links late-1930s appeasement to perceived British weakness, while treating the accompanying remembered quotation cautiously.

segments.title: Could stronger fleets prevent one overstretched world war?
segments.body: The scenario allows for war even if expanded fleets improve deterrence. Better crisis management could prevent European and Asia-Pacific conflicts from becoming one world war. Separate conflicts could place less strain on resources and allow forces to concentrate more effectively. Larger, better-balanced formations would have a wider range of supporting and defensive assets. In the argument here, that makes them harder to overwhelm and can reduce casualties compared with smaller exposed forces.

evidence.note: The proposed separation of European and Asia-Pacific conflicts, reduced resource strain, and the defensive advantages of larger balanced formations.

segments.summary: Separate European and Asia-Pacific conflicts could reduce overstretch and allow larger, better-balanced formations to operate.

segments.title: Why mutual cheating might discourage a war of aggression
segments.body: The prediction of continued peace rests partly on the treaty powers' initial reluctance to fight. Expanded fleets could make them feel more secure. Once each navy realized that its rivals were exploiting the same openings, however, its own apparent advantage would shrink. The resulting confidence in security is distinguished from confidence in winning a war of aggression.

evidence.note: The prediction that reciprocal evasion increases security without creating confidence in aggressive war.

segments.summary: Rival cheating could offset the apparent advantage of each navy's expansion while leaving it more secure.

segments.title: Japan and Germany face different effects from treaty evasion
segments.body: The Japanese case raises the question of whether greater confidence would reduce decisions driven by fear. Germany faces a different constraint because its fleet is governed by Versailles. Wider exploitation of Washington by other navies therefore does not offer Germany the same freedom. Instead, their expanded fleets could leave Germany in a worse relative position. The regional predictions depend on those different treaty and strategic circumstances.

evidence.note: Japan's possible response to greater confidence, and Germany's different position under Versailles.

segments.summary: Japan's confidence might change its decisions, while a German fleet still governed by Versailles would probably fall farther behind.

segments.title: France's Mediterranean and imperial commitments
segments.body: In this interpretation, France faces a choice between matching Italy in the Mediterranean and protecting its wider empire. Concentrating on the first commitment leaves France reliant on Britain for the second. That dependence adds pressure to an already difficult procurement position. Small carriers and other capabilities obtained through the proposed evasions could make France feel more capable of acting independently. Greater confidence is the suggested outcome, rather than a fully specified alternative French fleet.

evidence.note: France's Mediterranean competition with Italy, wider imperial commitments, dependence on Britain, and the proposed benefit of additional small carriers.

segments.summary: The argument treats France's split commitments as a source of dependence on Britain that wider treaty evasion could ease.

segments.title: Small carriers as support for distant or poorly equipped bases
segments.body: Small navies might adopt cruiser carriers once enough other countries demonstrated the type. Sweden and the Netherlands are suggested as possible followers. A mobile aviation platform could help address infrastructure limits at bases in the Baltic or Far East. The idea ends as an open question about whether those powers would copy the design. It does not specify which ships they would order or how fully a carrier would replace shore facilities.

evidence.note: Possible small-power adoption and the open question of carriers meeting infrastructure needs in the Baltic or Far East.

segments.summary: Sweden and the Netherlands introduce the possibility that small flight decks could help overcome limited base infrastructure.
